chunks: "Yes to all three, at different levels, so let me be specific. [C] : I've used C on [microcontroller / coursework] , where I wrote [GPIO, timer, UART, or an ISR] .
I'm comfortable with pointers, arrays, structs, bit manipulation for register access, and I know why a flag shared with an interrupt has to be volatile .
[C++] : I've used it for [a class project / simulator / driver] .
I understand classes, constructors and destructors, references versus pointers, and I've used the standard library containers like vector .
I'm less deep in templates and the more advanced features, so I'd call that intermediate. [Python] : this is what I use most for scripting, data analysis and test automation.
For example [parsing logs, plotting with matplotlib, driving an instrument] . I know lists, dictionaries, comprehensions, and file handling.
If one of these were new to me, I'd say so directly and point to the closest thing I've done.
For example, 'I haven't used C++ professionally, but I know C well, so pointers and memory are familiar and I'd pick up classes quickly.'
In general: C when I need control of memory and registers, Python when speed of development matters and performance doesn't, and C++ when I want abstraction without giving up C-like performance."
